title: Falafel
subtitle: crispy fried chickpea fritters
excerpt: Chickpeas, onion, garlic, and herbs blended together and fried into crispy golden balls. They are crunchy on the outside and bright green inside. Serve in flatbread with yoghurt and fresh vegetables.
sourceNotes: Falafel is eaten across the Middle East and North Africa. The chickpea version is most associated with Lebanese and Israeli cooking. It is one of the most popular street foods in the region.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze cooked falafel and reheat in an oven at 180C for 10 minutes.
recipe.batchNotes: Double the batch and freeze half.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the mixture a day ahead and refrigerate. Shape and fry just before eating.

content.text: Use dried chickpeas soaked overnight -- not tinned. Tinned chickpeas are too wet and the falafel will fall apart in the oil. The mixture should be dry enough to hold its shape when pressed into a ball.

items.prepNote: use 200g dried chickpeas, soaked overnight (not tinned -- they are too wet)

content.text: Drain the soaked chickpeas well. Pulse in a food processor with the onion, garlic, parsley, spices, salt, and baking powder.
Process until the mixture is a coarse paste -- not smooth. It should hold together when pressed.
Add flour if the mixture feels too wet. Refrigerate for 1 hour.
Shape into balls or discs about 3cm across.
Heat the oil in a wide pan over medium-high heat. Test with a small piece of mixture -- it should sizzle immediately.
Fry the falafel in batches for 3 to 4 minutes, turning, until golden brown all over.
Drain on kitchen paper and serve hot.

items.symptom: Falafel falls apart in the oil
items.fix: Add more flour and refrigerate longer. Make sure the mixture is firm when pressed. Test one falafel in the oil before cooking the rest.
Reduce the heat to medium. Falafel need 3 to 4 minutes per batch to cook all the way through.
Add more salt, cumin, and coriander to the mixture. Falafel needs bold seasoning.

content.text: Falafel is one of the most popular street foods across the Middle East and North Africa. Egypt's version uses fava beans. The Levantine version uses chickpeas. Both Israel and Lebanon claim it as their own national dish. Today falafel is eaten around the world and is one of the best examples of vegetarian food that does not feel like a compromise.
